name: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
title: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
answer: Historical role play, labeled as simulation, lets students interview or question a program that imagines a historical figure, a delegate at a constitutional convention, or a witness to an event. It builds curiosity and helps students see the past as lived by real people, but only when every simulation is clearly labeled and every quote is checked against a real source. Used carelessly, it spreads invented quotes and false history.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: The idea is to use a simulated historical figure as a partner for classroom questioning, so students can interview a figure, debate a delegate at a constitutional convention, or question a witness to an event. The problem it solves is distance, because a textbook can make the past feel finished and abstract while a conversation can make it feel like something people actually lived through. The risk it creates is equally real, since a program that imagines a person will also invent that person's words. The strict labeling and source checking rules exist to keep the curiosity without letting fabricated quotes pass as history. The teacher decides whether the activity is worth doing at all.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The teacher sets up the simulation and tests it before class, looking for obvious errors, so students meet a version that has already been checked once. In class, students interview the simulated figure, debate the simulated delegate, or question the simulated witness, and the activity is labeled clearly as a simulation so students know they are talking to a program imagining a person rather than the person. Any quote or claim a student wants to use must then be checked against a real source before it goes into their work. The text does not give separate grade bands for this idea, so the same sequence of setup, testing, labeling and source checking applies wherever it is used. The teacher also decides which figures and events are suitable for simulation in the first place.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its claims are about what careful use can do, building curiosity and helping students see the past as lived by real people, and about what careless use does, spreading invented quotes and false history. Those are judgments drawn from classroom experience rather than findings from a trial. Teachers and leaders should treat the idea as a practice to be tested locally, with the labeling and source checking rules treated as the conditions that make it defensible.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set out plainly. Every simulation must be labeled as a simulation, and any quote or claim students want to use must be checked against a real source. The teacher sets up and tests the simulation before class, looking for obvious errors. Some figures and events call for extra caution, because simulating people who suffered great injustice, such as enslaved people or victims of genocide, risks trivializing their experience or putting words in their mouths, and many teachers choose to avoid these simulations entirely and use real testimony instead. The decision about whether a simulation respects the people it represents stays with the teacher, not with the program.
